blocks.b:
Jim Marshall taught and played drums around London, and by 1960 he wanted a steadier living. He opened a shop, still mostly drums, called Jim and Terry Marshall at 76 Uxbridge Road, Hanwell. By 1962 a second shop had opened across the road, and the business had become J&T Marshall.

His drum pupils brought their guitarists in, among them Ritchie Blackmore, Jimmy Page and Pete Townshend. They told him they would rather buy guitars and amplifiers from him, because the West End shops treated them “like absolute idiots” for playing rock and roll.

Britain had kept American instruments out through the 1950s, and the big Fender amplifiers his customers wanted were scarce. Marshall imported what he could, but demand far outran supply. He turned to his repair technician Ken Bran, a guitarist he had hired from a repair job at Pan Am, and they chose Fender's late-1950s tweed Bassman, the 5F6-A, as the model.

Accounts differ on whether they copied a borrowed amplifier or worked from the schematic. An apprentice engineer from EMI helped with the design. The first prototype, late in 1962, followed the circuit closely but used British transformers, capacitors and resistors, and it brought in dozens of orders. Marshall recalled building amplifiers from Monday to Friday to sell in the shop on Saturday.

On the earliest heads the chassis was pushed to one end of the cabinet, and the front was covered in the same salt-and-pepper Vynair as the speaker grilles. The badge was a metal plate with MARSHALL in red enamel. It came from a Birmingham supplier of funeral goods, and it is still known as the coffin badge.

Inside, they copied the Bassman closely enough to keep its polarity switch, made for ungrounded American outlets and useless on British three-pin plugs. They kept its 5881 output valves. In the preamp they used the ECC83, the European 12AX7, in place of Fender's 12AY7. Each gave about two and a half times the gain, and the amplifier distorted sooner.

The production amplifiers of 1963 had the panel in the centre. Later that year came the sandwich front, with a black stripe across the top third. The polarity switch went and the panel read JTM 45 and MK II. The output valves later changed to British-made KT66s. Heads were sold as lead, bass and PA models, all essentially the same circuit.

By the end of 1963 the front was all black. The badge gave way to a silver Plexiglas plate with red letters, then to black letters on gold, and in 1965 to the script logo Marshall still uses. Panels of Traffolyte or aluminium gave way to Plexiglas the same year, first white, then gold. The head at the top of this chapter is a 1965 amplifier with the gold block logo.

Marshall built heads first and cabinets later. He recalled starting with two-by-twelves, but the 25-watt speakers of the day could not take an amplifier that peaked at around 70 watts, and they blew. He designed the smallest cabinet that would hold four 12-inch speakers. The first were Celestion G12 alnicos rated at 15 watts each. The ceramic G12M Greenback, at 20 watts, arrived in 1965 and was raised to 25 watts in 1968.

The cabinet was closed at the back, which gave a midrange punch unlike Fender's open-back combos. Dave Hunter, in The British Amp Invasion, calls the head on its 4x12 “the mightiest thing on the British stage” in 1963.

In 1964 Marshall added two combos built around the JTM45: the Model 1961 Super Tremolo with four 10-inch speakers, and the Model 1962 Lead and Bass with two 12s. In May 1966 Eric Clapton recorded with John Mayall's Bluesbreakers at Decca's studios in West Hampstead, playing a 1960 Les Paul through a Model 1962. The album came out in July, and the combo has been called the Bluesbreaker since.

The story that Clapton wanted an amp that fitted in the boot of his car is very likely false, since the combos were on sale before he used one. Which amp he played is not recorded, and Clapton has said he did not know what became of it.

By mid-1965 Pete Townshend's Fender amplifiers were not loud enough for the Who, and he asked Marshall for more. The JTM45/100 prototypes ran two 30-watt output transformers in parallel and a pair of GZ34 rectifiers, then a pair of 50-watt Drake transformers and four KT66s. The Who took several 100-watt heads in November 1965, with at least four cabinets holding eight 12-inch speakers each.

The eight-by-twelves soon gave way to two 4x12 cabinets, a straight one below and an angled one above. The 100-watt head became the Model 1959.

blocks.b:
Leo Fender never learned to play the guitar. He lost a job as an accountant in the Depression, had been repairing radios since he was 14, and opened the Fender Radio and Record Shop in Fullerton, California, where he also fixed amplifiers. After the single-speaker Champ and Deluxe, Fender added the Twin in 1952, first listed as the Twin 12 Amplifier and the Twin 12 Artist's Model.

The first version, the 5C8, had two 12-inch Jensen speakers and a pair of 6L6 output valves, and was rated at 25 watts. Its tweed cabinet had a new wide-panel front, with the grille cloth running between the inside edges of the box, and Fender called it its new “Hi Fidelity” amplifier.

Narrow-panel cabinets followed, with only thin strips of wood above and below the baffle. Dave Hunter, writing in Guitar & Bass, calls the early Twins “really just siblings of the Super and Pro amps”, with the same circuit and two 12-inch speakers, and notes that players who wanted more power often chose a Bassman.

By 1957 and 1958 the Twin used the 5E8A circuit, rated first at 40 and then at 80 watts. It ran two 5U4 rectifier valves, an unusual layout that reduced sag on hard-picked notes. Hunter says the tweed Twins are closer in sound and circuit to an early Marshall Bluesbreaker than to the Twin most players know today.

The tweed gave way to Tolex at the start of the 1960s. In 1961 the Twin came in white Tolex with a maroon grille cloth, with volume, treble and bass on the normal channel and volume, treble, bass, speed and intensity on the vibrato channel. A wheat grille arrived toward the end of 1962, and early in 1963 a black metal-reinforced handle replaced the brown one. Collectors still date these amps by their covering, grille and handle.

The Twin Reverb was introduced in late summer 1963. It was rated at 85 watts and had a silver-sparkle grille, a raised Fender logo and a new two-channel circuit, with bright switches on both channels in place of a presence control. The middle control came back, and the numbered, skirted knobs sat on a black panel, which is where the name blackface comes from.

The new features were spring reverb and a control Fender labelled vibrato. It varied the volume rather than the pitch, so it was a tremolo. The tweed and blonde Twins had different circuits and no reverb at all.

Hunter calls the blackface Twin Reverb “the benchmark design”, the most powerful large professional guitar amplifier then sold by a major maker. Where other Fenders began to break up at about 4 on the volume knob, a Twin Reverb stayed clean to about 6 or 7. That suited bands playing big stages without microphones on the amps, and it left a clean base for effects pedals. The amplifier weighed 35 kilograms or more.

It could still roar when it was turned up. Michael Bloomfield played a blackface Twin Reverb on his recordings with the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, photographs from the 1960s show Keith Richards with blackface Twin Reverbs, and the Beatles used Twin Reverbs for the Apple rooftop performance.

Leo Fender sold the company to CBS in 1965. The silverface Twin Reverb followed in late 1967 or 1968, depending on the account, with a brushed aluminium panel and a blue-sparkle grille. The early silverface circuit changed the bias and phase inverter and added seven parts to the output stage, and the rating rose to 100 watts.

A master volume arrived in 1972, and the rating reached 135 watts in 1977. Harry Hank of Hank's Vintage Guitars says the master volume and boost controls turned the clean amp with lots of headroom into a dirtier, less responsive one. The black panel returned as an option in 1980 and was standard by 1982, the last year of the traditional Twin Reverb. Fender later reissued the 1965 version.
